newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - CPI, retail sales and the Fed.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - CPI, retail sales and the Fed.

text.p: Uncertainty about what the Federal Reserve will do next has the U.S. credit markets anxiously awaiting the release of two key economic indicators on Friday, analysts said.
At 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Friday, the government will release the consumer price index (CPI) and the retail sales report, both for the month of August.
In a Reuters survey, U.S. economists see overall and core (ex-food and energy prices) CPI posting a 0.2 percent rise. The overall and core CPI rose 0.3 percent in July.
Retail sales are seen up 0.7 percent in August while the ex-autos number is forecast to rise 0.4 percent, against a 0.1 percent increase and a 0.3 percent jump in July, respectively.

"Those indicators are expected to be key to defining the course of monetary policy in September," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank. "The market is divided now and people will be scrutizing the numbers, looking for cues."

Anlysts said the release of a benign producer price index (PPI) report Thursday prompted market players to question the apparent consensus that the Fed would raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points in September.

They said there are now two clear lines of thought in the market -- the ones who believe in a tightening as a pre- emptive strike against inflation and those who think the Fed might take advantage of "opportunistic disinflation."
Analysts said the real showdown is expected to take place at the next meeting of the Federal Open Market Commitee (FOMC) on September 24.
They said some Fed officials are now perceived to be willing to experiment with the idea that higher growth alone does not necessarily mean more inflation down the road.
But they added there are members of the FOMC perceived to be in favor of acting in a traditional sense, which is to react when labor markets get tighter and wages accelarate.

"I think it's the opportunistic disinflation camp versus the tradional camp," said Patrick Dimick, economist at C.S. First Boston. "And it's hard to say who's is going to win ... At this point our position is that the Fed will not raise rates (on September 24)," Dimick added.
Despite recent fears of rising inflation, the Bureau of Labor Statistics announced Thursday the U.S. core PPI was down 0.1 percent in August. The overall number rose 0.3 percent.

"I don't think accelarating inflation is innevitable and, in fact, we think the economy is slowing and that will staunch any tendency for inflation to rise," said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities Inc.
Levenson said he expects the Fed will stand pat in September. "The (no action) sentiment has grown, but it is still a minority view," the economist said.
Indeed, many economists still believe the Fed will not refrain from raising rates in September. "I think they will raise by 25 (basis points)," said Paul Kasriel, economist at Northern Trust.

"But I don't think they will raise the discount rate, which would play into the story that they are is just taking back the January insurance they bought earlier in the year," he added, referring to the Fed's 25 basis point cut in the federal funds rate in January.
On Thursday, the benchmark 30-year U.S. T-bond was up 14/32 at 95-31/32 in late trading to yield 7.08 percent.

The Fed added reserves to the money market on Thursday via seven-day fixed system repurchase agreements. Federal funds are seen opening at 5.19 percent on Friday, below the Fed's 5-1/4 percent target. -- 212-859-1676
